units.text: Oral history as an analytical tool: Eve Mahlab and the Australian Trailblazing Women Law Project

In using the term 'citizenship', we are thinking in particular of the practice of law in the public sphere in its many varied possible expressions, as embodied by solicitors, barristers and judges in public policy and law and/or business and law, by government lawyers at a domestic and international level, and by parliamentary drafters, legal researchers and academics.In addition, we include those individuals who, like Eve Mahlab, trained in law and took a different career path, but nevertheless applied their skills, training and authority to effect legal and policy reform. 3Each of these roles exists as important parts of public life and civic activity, fitting within an understanding of citizenship as public civic participation. 4 The early narratives recorded in the pilot series enabled the research team to test and hone the project's methodology and analytical foci.Building on the pilot, the ARC Trailblazing Project has now reached its goal of recording a further forty-five interviews with women lawyers who represent a diversity of life experience in terms of age, ethnicity, geography, legal community and type of legal role.Through a range of outputs, including an online exhibition, 5 conferences and other public events, and research completed by Louise Baker, the TBWL PhD student, 6 the project showcases and has begun to analyse the first publicly accessible 7 oral history of seven decades of Australia's pioneer, 'trailblazing' women lawyers. 8
Aim and objectives of the paper

Having achieved some of the project's key milestones, this piece revisits some of the TBWL data to re-examine the project's core tenets and research questions, as elaborated below (2.1).Eve Mahlab's oral history has been chosen from among the pilot interviews, above all because it highlights the diversity of pioneering Australian women lawyers' formative influences and contributions as active citizens; and additionally, because of her especially candid and intimate account of the intersection of these influences on the shaping of her markedly divergent and trailblazing path in the professional, civic and private spheres. 9he analysis of Eve Mahlab's life narrative thus has two principal objectives: first, it argues that it is vital that this diversity be recognised, in research and public consciousness, as significant not only to the history of women's rights but to an understanding of active citizenship.To this end, the paper examines a range of influences on Eve's civic participation-including the intersection of gender, generation and personality with family background, ethnicity, religion, citizenship status and education, legal training and authority-and draws at times on comparative data from the stories of other Australian trailblazing lawyers, especially those of her generation, to provide a socio-historical and cultural context for viewing Mahlab's life and achievements.Second, the paper seeks to legitimate oral history as a methodology in legal research and to demonstrate its unique value in making us privy to trailblazers' personal insights, because, unlike memoir and auto-/biography, it can do so with an authenticity that comes from hearing and interpreting first-hand the inflections of the interviewee's voice, a quality that can add depth to, transcend or even problematise the words on the written transcript.And it can do so with an immediacy than can be explored, challenged and/or reflected on by and with the interviewee.
Outline of the paper

The paper begins with a brief description of the Trailblazing Project, focusing in 2.1 on its goal-namely, the need to address the knowledge gap around pioneer women lawyers' participation in Australian citizenship-and principal objectives, which are framed in terms of the disciplinary and analytical breakthroughs the project is seeking to achieve.The key research questions developed and mapped through each narrative recorded in the Trailblazing Project are introduced in 2.2, followed in 2.3 by a description of theoretical and practical aspects of the methodology adopted in the project-the recording and critical analysis, from multi-disciplinary perspectives, of oral histories.The paper then draws on Eve Mahlab's oral history to provide a biographical overview of her personal and professional life and acts of citizenship (Section 3).Section 4 comprises a close analysis of the interview that has three foci: first, formative influences on Eve's life and career (Section 4.1), particularly her social and educational background and interactions with law; second, key instances of Eve's contribution of advocacy for social and legal reform towards the equality and empowerment of women (4.2); and third, discussion of Eve's self-perception of her contributions to public life (4.3).The findings from this in-depth examination of the text in the conclusion provide responses to some of TBWL's research questions, including what they reveal about continuity and change in the legal and wider social culture, and similarities and divergence in women's self-perception as civic actors-or active citizens.

The paper concludes by arguing that the recording and analysis of life narratives such as Eve Mahlab's (and the larger group of TBWL interviews) will ultimately inform our understanding of citizenship and of how social action, in particular that of women lawyers, will reshape the public civic space. 10 Background: the Trailblazing Women and the Law Project
Goal and principal objectives of the project

Trailblazing women lawyers stand at the professional forefront of women's participation in Australian civic life.Their position is exceptional, important and ground-breaking; yet, there were few references in public records to many of the women interviewed, despite their being well known in their field. 11he primary reasons for this situation are historical and deeply rooted in traditional social and cultural values, as well as earlier institutional discrimination.As Mary Jane Mossman wrote of the first women lawyers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, whereas 'the role of women doctors could be explained as an extension of women's roles in the "private sphere", women lawyers were clearly "intruding on the public domain explicitly reserved to men"'. 12The result, as Kim Rubenstein has previously written, is that Australia is far from achieving an equality of women's participation in the legal landscape and is still working towards full citizenship for women in the civic legal world. 13ence, the project's overall goal is that the detrimental and well-noted silence surrounding the first women of law in Australia be exploded by combining a cross-section of disciplinary questioning to build a national consciousness of women lawyers and to enable critical research of their diverse experiences.By exploring the merit of this 'post-structural turn' on oral history, we foreground the storytelling of legal practitioners as an important method of legal research, responding to parallel, 'ethno-historical' research approaches which advocate the uniqueness of legal participants' stories in revealing the contours of law as a social institution. 14Fundamentally, this work forms a new empirical basis for theorising the value of oral history to legal research.By recording and analysing these unheard narratives, the project has the potential not only to enable us to better understand trailblazing and oral history methods further, but to tap and broadcast the wealth of experience possessed by living trailblazers to inform the way we think about gender and citizenship in Australia.

While addressing the overarching knowledge gap described above, at its outset, the Trailblazer Project focused on four areas of enquiry where the picture of Australian legal women was, until then, sparse, but especially important.

First, we attempted to develop a historical picture of Australian women's experiences upon entering the legal profession. 15Second, a key objective of this research was to ensure that the diversity of women lawyers' trailblazing experiences was recognised in research and public consciousness. 16This objective was addressed by recording and then intricately detailing the difference and consistency of trailblazers' experiences across the nation and profession.By positing diversity as a core tenet of the research, the Trailblazing Project has generated a much more demographically complex picture of women trailblazers across generations, jurisdictions and practices and ethnic, marital and religious statuses. 17This data allows us to comprehensively interrogate these women's perceptions of the impact of diverse factors on their lived experience.As Mossman has written of women in the Canadian legal system, 'the "glass ceiling" was often experienced by minority women as a "steel door"'. 18racing these differences in women lawyers' experiences is essential to responding to the hypotheses that pioneer women lawyers' lives are heavily contoured by their professional and social backgrounds; 19 to contradicting the traditional presentation and study of women as a unitary class; and to ultimately opening up new ways to move towards an equality of citizenship in the legal profession.

A third objective of the project was to undertake a detailed, national, academic study of the connections between trailblazers to other organisations through professional, familial or social associations, since many existing stories of trailblazing in Australia, particularly in individual biographies, had emphasised the singular, non-strategic elements of pioneer women's successes. 20
Research questions

The research questions formulated for TBWL were designed to inform our understanding of public spaces, citizenship and lawyering, and therefore to address the central question of the role played by women lawyers in broadening our conception of active citizenship in the public sphere.Those of particular relevance to Eve Mahlab's story are the following:

. How has the intersection of gender with ethnicity, age, religion, location and type of legal practice influenced the way trailblazing women lawyers experience and retell their lives at the 'legal frontier' and in public life? .Have women lawyers chosen law because of its reform potential in relation to gender equality? .How have these women used their legal training to political effect and how effective has the influence of women lawyers as public actors been in socio-legal reform towards an equality of citizenship for women? .In their estimation, has the professional authority and public influence accorded to lawyers enhanced these women's civic authority? .What do the trailblazers' different ways of retelling their experiences reveal about their position within the legal and national culture?
Method

From a theoretical perspective, the innovative approach adopted in the Trailblazing Project in response to the situation described above, involves the application of oral history to the history and analysis of law as a social and political institution on a scale unprecedented in Australia.Oral history as a method that both captures and generates data is essential in our case because, until now, as discussed in 2.1 above and as argued by Jill Kerr Conway 21 and Mossman, 22 the personal histories of pioneer women within the professions have been largely absent from public discussion in Australia.In this sense, our methodology is novel and restorative, since it treats oral histories as texts upon which to draw and to question, departing from the traditional treatment in gender and law analyses of the narrative as primarily a source for compiling data on types of experience (e.g.promotion or discrimination). 23While the TBWL oral histories are not statistically representative, patterns of continuity and change in the legal and national contexts emerge from the stories of women from diverse generations, locations, cultural, ethnic and religious backgrounds.Thus, the application of this method allows for a clawing back of subjectivity for participants within the legal context.In its practice of oral history, the Trailblazing Project transcends and complicates the traditional disciplinary conception of oral history as a scholarly 'panacea designed to fill in the blanks in … women's history', or provide a 'purer version of the past coming unadulterated from the very person who experienced it'. 24In addition, oral history interviews are treated as a unique co-construction of the interaction between the interviewee, the interviewer and the questions asked during the interview.Describing the oral interview an 'interactional accomplishment', 25 Mlynář emphasises that its 'cogency as evidence of the past, as well as its power as a document of personal experience, originate "in the act of oral, face-to-face communication"'. 26Valerie Raleigh Yow further reminds us of the need for reflectivity about the relationship between the interviewer and interviewee:

liking or not liking, feeling repelled by difference in ideology or attracted by a shared worldview, sensing difference in gender or age or social class or ethnicity, all influence the ways we ask questions and respond to narrators and interpret and evaluate what they say. 27opting this approach generates accounts of the interviewee's experience that tell us far more than recounted facts.As Caroline Daley writes, '[w]hat women remember and retell, and how they retell it, tells us much about their individual experiences and their understanding of their cultural place with their community'. 28In this sense too, the analysis of the TBWL oral histories is enriched by discourse analysis, as in this paper on Eve Mahlab and in studies of the oral histories of two trailblazing international lawyers, Erika Feller, 29 in the realm of public law, and Rosemary Kayess, in that of disability law. 30e nevertheless acknowledge that oral history as a genre has attracted 'fierce debates' about 'the reliability of memory, the psychology of the interview relationship … [and] the interpretation and reinterpretation of people's lives'. 31The measures outlined below represent an attempt to address some of these contested aspects.

From a more practical perspective, in the case of both the pilot and main Trailblazing interviews, the interviewer followed Yow's advice-that everything done before the interview will contribute to establishing the nature of the interviewer-interviewee relationship. 32To this end, a preliminary meeting was held, at which time interviewees were provided with a series of chronologically structured questions and points to consider in advance of the interview.The interviewer also had a research assistant prepare a chronology that drew from material provided by the interviewee and from an extensive online search of any publicly available material.The chronology focused on influences-including, gendered influences-on the interviewees of their family, education, legal training and career.The actual interview was then conducted as a conversation, with the interviewer further exploring the interviewees' answers to the background questions. 33Oral history interviews depend on the interviewer, interviewee and end-users sharing such topically specific historical information, along with linguistically universal knowledge related to each participant's language competence. 34n addition, the fact that the Trailblazing interviews were conducted over several days enabled both participants to reflect on topics discussed during the earlier conversation, resulting in a more dynamic and co-constructive data production process.The dynamic nature of the interview process thus enabled the interviewees to comment on, modify or amplify their recorded material in the course of the interview, as well as in conversation after.For instance, Eve Mahlab's oral history was recorded over the course of two days and communication between the interviewee and interviewer continued beyond this time. 35In addition, once complete, the interviews were transcribed by NLA staff and sent back to the interviewee for spelling corrections of places and names only.The interviewee could also add a note to the transcript if there was a factual mistake identified, but the oral history recording itself was not changed as it is a record of that conversation. 36urthermore, the interviewees maintained 'control' over whether their interviews became publicly accessible.

Discourse analysis of Eve's oral history involved a number of steps: first, repeated close reading of the transcript with a focus, at the macro-level, on sections of the text of most relevance to the aims of the project and the objectives of this paper; comparison of these findings with the specific research questions listed in 2.2; and discussion of findings by the authors.At a micro-level, the analysis involved identification and itemised recording of recurring motifs in the narrative; and at an even more fine-grained level, of salient patterns of language use (e.g.expressions of obligation, as discussed in 4.1.4and 4.3.1 below) which, in the model developed by Anne Isaac, form characteristic features of Eve's 'voice' that portray her in certain ways. 37Following this model of voice, we attended most closely to expressions of attitude, since these are widely considered to be the closest linguistic indices of identity.

Second, close listening to inflections in Eve's acoustic voice in selected segments of the audio recording of the interview made it possible to confirm, modify or dismiss impressions of identity gathered from the above-mentioned voice analysis of the transcript.For instance, the audio recording amplified the self-judgemental tone of Eve's reflections on her qualities as a mother (see 4.1.6below).
Eve Mahlab AO: biographical overview

What follows is a snapshot of a life directed to contribution in a range of expressions of public activity, representing citizenship in its broader participatory sense. 38This sets the context for thinking further about the place of law in enabling women to participate in public life in ways that enlarge our concept of active citizenship.Eve Mahlab's pioneering career began at the age of twenty-two, when she graduated with a law degree from the University of Melbourne, Victoria, in 1959, followed by the completion of her articles in a family law (then known as 'matrimonial causes') practice.She was later admitted as a barrister and solicitor, then moved to Sydney, New South Wales (NSW) shortly after her marriage to Frank Mahlab, an American business executive, and worked in the NSW Public Solicitor's Office in a section that was a precursor to Legal Aid (a free, government-funded legal advice service).These 'women's work' contexts-to which other Australian trailblazing lawyers were confined in the 1960s and 1970s-gave Eve further experience in family law-related matters, but also an informal, 'on the ground' training in advocacy, particularly where advising female clients of their legal rights was concerned.Indeed, her early experience as a lawyer could be said to have helped shape Eve's social and feminist consciousness, with the added irony that her position at the Public Solicitor's Office came to an abrupt halt when she was not allowed to return to work because she once fainted when pregnant.This incident highlights some of the formal barriers faced by women lawyers of Eve's generation, who, in some cases, were even forced to resign as soon as they were married-and the informal barriers to the full participation of female lawyers of succeeding generations, as evidenced in the cases of Peg Lusink, Erika Feller and Valerie French-because of both the networking culture in law firms that intentionally and/or effectively excluded married women with family responsibilities, and gender-related conservative attitudes within the legal profession and Australian society more broadly. 39ve's career was put on hold for the next four years when she returned to Melbourne to give birth to her first child in 1961 and subsequently, two more children, in 1963 and 1964.She soon resumed work, practising family law from home, but found balancing the needs of her young children and her practice challenging and frustrating.Finding interesting part-time work in a legal practice proved equally difficult.Juggling motherhood and work raised Eve's awareness to the fact that other married women lawyers wishing to remain in the workforce must have shared her experience.In 1968, drawing on her entrepreneurial instinct and knowledge of the Melbourne legal landscape, Eve founded Mahlab Recruitment as an employment agency placing female lawyers in law firms.The agency's clientele was subsequently expanded to include male lawyers and then accountants and architects seeking employment.Her business acumen, success and confidence led Eve to open an office in Sydney in 1970, and then, because of the fluctuating nature of the recruitment business, to branch out into publishing specialist diaries for lawyers, followed by diaries for accountants and builders, and later still, into legal costing.

While it is more common today for lawyers to apply their knowledge and skills in domains other than the practice of law, Eve's career shift was an unusual one fifty years ago.Her entrepreneurial activities represent a significant departure from the traditional route for lawyering, particularly in the 1960s when most men would have continued working as solicitors in law firms or moved fully to the bar to work as a barrister in the Courts.Although she maintained a practising certificate for many years and was involved in reviving the Women Lawyer's Association, she ceased practising law and instead used her legal background to service the legal profession, a form of active citizenship that showcases the diverse range of contributions to the public sphere by trailblazing women lawyers interviewed as part of the TBWL project.

As a self-employed businesswoman, and with the support of her husband, who had given up work as a senior executive at Ford to share child-rearing duties and work from home in other endeavours, Eve was able to structure her own time and engage in other activities.While she considered herself to be 'liberated', 40 her feminist consciousness was not fully awakened until she joined the recently formed Women's Electoral Lobby (WEL) in 1972.The political orientation of WEL's approach to feminist issues appealed to Eve, as did its founding members, a group of young 'very savvy' 41 women academics, who, in turn, recognised Eve's legal and advocacy skills and entrepreneurial talent, enabling her to bring all these abilities together in her work around women's rights.Eve's description of her introduction to WEL almost forty years later still conveys the immediacy and depth of her sense of belonging with these women: I went to a meeting that I saw advertised in The Nation Review, which was a paper at that time.And Beatrice Faust, and some other incredible women, held this meeting.And I thought, 'I've found my home.' 42 Eve was initially tasked with using her legal training to redraft WEL's constitution, but as her commitment to the group grew and as the group recognised that she was both articulate and assertive, she became its unofficial media contact person and participated in advocacy to address discrimination against women in employment and to reform the grounds for divorce in the Commonwealth Matrimonial Causes Act (later repealed and renamed the Family Law Act in 1975). 43Her considerable entrepreneurial, leadership, lobbying 44 and networking skills also came to the fore in the WEL Forum in 1973, where politicians were invited to answer women's questions to decide who they would vote for in the upcoming Victorian state election.

By 1975, the confidence and prominence Eve Mahlab had gained through her participation in WEL opened the door to further opportunities to contribute acts of citizenship in the public sphere.She was appointed to the Victorian Inquiry into the Status of Women, a committee whose report led to the introduction of anti-discrimination legislation.She also became the first woman elected to Monash University's Council, serving for six years on a number of its committees and advocating for equal opportunity and family-friendly policies, particularly childcare, since it 'empowered women to move into the workforce'. 45Her civic activity extended directly into party politics where she joined the Liberal Party of Australia and learned to make the speeches and connections required in the world of politics.However, after three unsuccessful attempts at pre-selection she also determined it was not a direction of public activity that she was committed to pursuing.

Eve's contributions in other areas of civic life in the service of government, business and the community more broadly have been extensive, varied and mostly voluntary: in 1979, she represented Victoria at the Australian Plan of Action Conference (convened to determine the national agenda to be taken to the UN Decade for Women), leading a coalition of anti-conservative groups that advocated women's rights to reproductive freedom and their access to safe abortion.In 1982, at the age of forty-five, Eve was named the Australian Businesswoman of the Year.The award provided her with opportunities to extend her business interests and network, as well as a platform for childcare advocacy, with real effect.By 1985, she had co-founded an Australian branch of an international organisation for women business owners (Femmes Chefs d'Entreprise) and founded the 'KnowBis' business education project in Victoria.In the following decade, Eve was also a trailblazer in being a woman appointed to a string of boards in the public sector (the Victorian State Training Board in 1988; the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute for Medical Research in 1990; the Film Australia Board in 1998); the Jewish community (the Jewish Commission for the Future, 1991); and the corporate sector (where she became the first woman elected to, and remunerated for her work on, the Westpac Banking Corporation board).In 1995, during her term on the Westpac board (1993-2002), Eve attended the Fourth UN World Conference on Women in Beijing.In 1998, she was approached by the Victorian Women's Trust to lead the women's ticket to ensure more women were elected to the Constitutional Convention on the question of whether Australia should become a Republic.

Recognition of Eve Mahlab's significant contributions to public life has taken the form of awards-including the Order of Australia for services to business, government and the community, particularly for services to women (1988); a Monash University Honorary Doctorate (1997); and a Centenary Medal for service to the community through business and commerce (2001)-and her appointment by the Prime Minister as an ambassador for honouring women (2002).Again, such recognition for a woman was, and remains, unusual. 46Now in her eighties, Eve remains active in public affairs and social issues, with a particular commitment to the Australian Women Donors Network which she co-founded in 2007 47 to promote philanthropic initiatives designed to build 'a better world through women and girls'. 48
Examining the text: findings

This section looks more closely at the transcript of Eve's oral history, and in keeping with the foci of the paper (see 1.2 above), foregrounds three major themes: formative influences on her life, her interactions with law in particular; her acts of citizenship; and her self-perception of the nature of her contributions to the public sphere.Recurring motifs within these themes are highlighted to show how they respond to specific research questions posed in the Trailblazing Project.
Formative influences

Eve Mahlab's interview provides an in-depth, candid, first-hand portrayal of the dominant influences and challenges in her personal and professional life, allowing us to trace the growth of her social, especially feminist, consciousness and better understand the motivations for her acts on the public stage.
Family background

Eve was born in Vienna, Austria, in 1937, the only child of Robert and Gertrud (Trudi) Dickstein (later anglicised to Dickens) the year before the Anschluss. 49Soon after her birth, her Jewish parents were evicted from their home and forced into hiding in a hotel attic in Vienna.Like many Viennese Jews, her family had identified more with their citizenship and culture than with their religion.Both her parents' families were successful entrepreneurs and, as such, were used to exercising their rights as citizens and their influence.Indeed, when her maternal grandfather, Arthur Albers, was taken by the Nazis to a detention centre (Bukenwalt), Eve's mother secured his release by waiting 'outside the building of … the Gestapo to see anybody that she could influence … to have him released'. 50Albers, a timber merchant and exporter, who Eve describes as 'the towering figure' in her family, refused to relinquish his assets in foreign bank accounts and used his commercial contacts to outsmart the Nazis. 51Like her mother's 'heroic' achievement, 52 her grandfather's decision to fight the Nazis' demands, as a matter of principle, highlights the strength of character and sense of authority and entitlement in her family background that for her 'set an example … of fighting … ' and asserting her rights. 53Voice analysis of Eve's description of this episode underlines the force of her rejection of powerlessness, oppression and inequality.

In 1939, Eve and her parents arrived in Australia as enemy aliens on visas obtained by her father's sister and husband, who had immigrated earlier, as theirs had been one of the first Jewish businesses taken over by the Nazis.Eve was two when her family settled in Melbourne and started up a cottage industry making dolls at the property they rented.Soon after, she began attending kindergarten, so that she could 'learn to speak English and become Australian'. 54
Schooling

Eve did not recall her school years 'with any … enjoyment', 55 particularly those spent at two private girls' schools.Her later primary school years were interrupted by a year spent with her parents in New York, where her maternal grandparents had lived since leaving Vienna.However, the family were not happy in America and on her return, Eve recalled feeling 'very insecure' which made her 'show off a lot'. 56This reinforced her self-perception as a 'social outcast' and earned her a reputation as a 'trouble maker'. 57Eve experienced both girls' schools as 'repressive institutions' 58 that left her with a 'feeling of powerlessness … ' 59 :

We were expected to conform.… it was like … being on an assembly line … it was just walking everywhere in double files and going to assembly and not having real discussions with teachers, you know, … listening more than having good discussions.I just didn't fit in with … institutional life, that's all … . 60 report from an aptitude test Eve took at the age of fourteen provides a telling picture of her capacity and strong-mindedness, as well as of her need for application and guidance:

There would be very few in the general population who would obtain results equal to or better at Eve's age of fourteen years.In fact, she's one of the most capable girls I have ever met.However, whilst Eve has a natural capacity to do any professional training course, it is well for her to remember that constant application would be necessary as well as a more systematic and … a neat setting out of her work.For her age, she is most mature.She has a most likeable personality and, at the moment, is likely to prove a little difficult in her adjustment to family life.With some careful guidance, encouragement, she should do well. 61
Identification with Judaism

A more positive outcome of her experience of her 'otherness' during her adolescence was the development of a Jewish identity, which began through her friendship with Jewish students in secondary school-' … there were Chinese girls and there were Jewish girls.And the Chinese girls tended to mix together and the Jewish girls tended to mix together' 62 -and subsequently with a circle of Jewish friends outside school.As a child, Eve 'didn't even know' she was Jewish.This consciousness 'just sort of seeped in gradually … I can't remember how I got this feeling and stories about Vienna and the Nazis'. 63However, as refugees who had lost their Austrian citizenship, her parents wanted Eve to have Jewish friends.Eve's identification with Judaism and the history of Jewish people took on a greater importance later in her life with the growth of her social consciousness and her advocacy of equal opportunity, since she was able to recognise strong parallels between the situation of Jews and that of women.

I think there's a lot that Jews and women have in common … They're both groups that have suffered … disadvantage and discrimination.And they're both groups that have worked towards emancipation, right?… I always felt there was a lot that the women's movement, or women, could learn from the Jews.And the biggest thing is the importance of your history.

… you see … women … have a history but it's not available, right?And for the Jews, our history, I think, gives enormous strength and framework to understanding the world around us and our place in it.And I think it contributes to the stability of our communities and, on an individual level, to the contribution that so many people who come from a Jewish culture make to the world. 64e importance of Eve's identification with Judaism contrasts with the experience of other trailblazers of Jewish origin, including Peg Lusink, who were either born in Australia or whose family arrived in Australia prior to World War II; or who, like Erika Feller, had a parent who had escaped the Holocaust and soon became assimilated into mainstream Australian culture (see 4.1.4below).
Parental influences

As an only child, Eve's relationship with her parents was especially intense.On the one hand, she was brought up to be independent, as her refugee parents were preoccupied in making a living and remaking their lives in Australia.Comparing her own upbringing with the level of parental support expected of subsequent generations, Eve commented: 'My parents, … were doing other things.… I don't remember discussing things that happened with my parents.You know, I just got on with it'. 65On the other hand, she was aware, particularly when she was younger, of her parents' expectations of her to achieve in her career 'to regain … what they had lost in status and position'. 66n contrast, this sensitivity to her social and citizenship status as the child of refugees is again absent in the narratives of Peg Lusink and Erika Feller, both from families in which women and men practised in professions that accorded them social status and authority. 67ve's 'getting of wisdom' and search for self-expression and fulfilment through different public and personal identities can be seen in terms of these two conflicting impulses: self-determination on the one hand, and, on the other, the need to 'do better than anyone else' 68 and achieve social recognition to satisfy parental expectations and overcome the 'second-rate citizen' 69 status that is synonymous with 'the migrant experience'. 70These opposing impulses were accentuated by her parents' very traditional attitude to gender differences.Eve recalls her mother saying '"the most important thing for a woman is to be attractive for a man"'. 71In this sense, she was subject to the 'conventions of the fifties' and beyond that Jill Ker Conway described as identifying 'marriage and child rearing [as] the only acceptable female achievements'. 72t the same time, Eve was also shaped by differences in her relationship with each of her parents.Eve admired her mother's intelligence and the entrepreneurial drive that 'fuelled' the family's business ventures, as well as Trudi's 'need for growth and activity' that led her to become a real estate agent, a 'radical' move for a woman of her culture and time. 73But, perhaps because of their similarity, the relationship between mother and daughter was conflictual, even competitive.Her father, however, recognised and validated Eve's intellectual capacity, her articulateness, and also accepted her fierce independence and stubbornness: I did have a lot of, I guess, conflict with my mother but an enormous amount of support from my father, who always said he knew I was difficult.And he accepted that.… He said, because I was difficult and no man would put up with me … and I would probably not get married so I would have to support myself (emphasis added). 74r these reasons, Robert Dickens concluded that Eve should study law: 'So, if he said I should do law, I did law' (emphasis added). 75Similarly, articles were 'something that had to be done.… I took it that I wanted to be a solicitor' (emphasis added). 76haracterised by expressions of obligation (should, have/had to), this refrain is present throughout her discussion of her upbringing, schooling ('you had to sit in these smelly cloakrooms to have your lunch' 77 ), and even her motivations to marry ('Suddenly my parents … said I had to get married' 78 ) (emphasis added).It is equally present in her description of the completion of her law degree and articles, her registration as a solicitor, her admission to the bar and early career in family law related matters, first in Melbourne and later in the Public Solicitor's Office in Sydney.These expressions suggest a powerlessness, or, at least, a lack of conscious choice that plays into the powerlessness/empowerment dynamic that later became a key driver of Eve's professional and civic activity.The use of verbs of obligation could also be considered to index Eve's social background as the child of parents who had lost the equality that comes with full citizenship and so placed 'strong pressure' on her to succeed, while simultaneously holding traditional attitudes to women's roles. 79Again, for the reasons given earlier, Eve's social background contrasts with those of Peg Lusink, born twelve years ahead of Eve, and Erika Feller, born twelve years after Eve.
Generational context: prevailing social attitudes towards and expectations of women

In addition, the analysis of her recollections of the early part of her life indicates that despite her outspoken and rebellious nature, Eve Mahlab in many ways unconsciously conformed to traditional expectations of women of her generation and cultural context.As Nancy Knauer points out, '[o]ur individual identity and worldview are the unique product of a particular historical context', and while identity formation 'involves constant reinterpretation and reinvention', prevailing public attitudes at the time an individual comes of age are likely to have a profound influence on the development of that person's sense of self and worldview. 80Knauer's thesis helps to explain the resonance, throughout Eve Mahlab's narrative, of contemporary attitudes towards a woman's place in society, of her adolescent perceptions of her parents' conflicting expectations of her as a woman, and, as discussed below, and of her sense of her otherness at school and university.

Thus, for instance, she was in the minority when, in 1954, at the very young age of sixteen, she entered the University of Melbourne Law School, a very male domainshe was one of only seven females in a cohort of eighty or ninety students-and while she 'tended to be fairly opinionated' and vocal and had closer male than female friends, she was not attracted to the 'pub-crawling and … drunken social life' of many male students. 81Her sense of being an outsider to this culture was exacerbated by being referred to in the law students' magazine as 'the girl with the … bouncy breasts or something like that'. 82Although she had no theory of feminism at the time, the comment 'stifled' her and made her 'self-conscious' 'for a long time'. 83ve's comments about the sexual harassment and gender discrimination she experienced in law school echoes the testimonies, not only of other trailblazers of her generation 84 -even though these women did not have then the vocabulary we have today to name such experiences-but also of those of the next generation, 85 both in Australia and internationally. 86One result of her 'practical exclusion' from the male student culture was a lack of 'conversation' around and understanding of 'the framework of the legal profession'. 87Thus, whereas Eve did her articles in 'a small family law firm' 88 -'traditional women's stuff' 89 -her male friends, many from business families, knew about the avenues available to law graduates who chose to do their articles in the big law firms.

I don't think I was party to the conversations that law students had about where to go for articles.And they probably had it with their lecturers as well.… I don't know whether it was just me, and I don't know whether it was because I was a woman, but it just wasn't part of my planning, my career planning.And it's also possible that maybe my career wasn't as important to me, for all sorts of social reasons, as it was to the boys. 90e's recollections resonate with further testimonies in the TBWL collection, which indicate that, as recently as the 1990s, female lawyers who were ethnically, socio-economically and culturally different were doubly disadvantaged in respect of the networking culture and the 'boys' club' at university. 91In reflection, although the familial and broader social forces mentioned above shaped and constrained Eve Mahlab's career directions, they also contributed to her growing awareness of gender inequality, as discussed below.
Marriage and motherhood

Working in a family law practice had sensitised Eve to the disadvantages faced by women seeking a divorce, which was then based on fault.It taught her that despite legal reform in this area, women continue to be: time-poor … money-poor and … confidence-poor, compared to men.… So basically, if women want access to the justice system, they have to go to the private … legal system.And … they're at a disadvantage 'cause the fees are extraordinarily high. 92wever, as for many women, it was in relation to her roles as a wife and mother that Eve, became acutely aware of the juxtaposition between who she was and traditional expectations of a woman.

Eve Mahlab overwhelmingly expresses gratitude and amazement for the 'enormously important' role her husband, Frank, played in her life and career: I don't know how I lucked into marrying the man I did.But Frank has always been supportive.He … anchors me.… I have enormous respect for his abilities, which complement mine … and his intelligence and his interest.I mean, we really have a lot of discussions about big issues, probably things we can't change.But, I mean, he writes letters off about climate change and various things even at this stage when he's eighty.But we've always been involved in, in community activities and interested in public issues. 93r use of the idiom 'lucked into' here reinforces the fact that, during that period and beyond, women did not expect that men contribute or participate equally in raising a family. 94n the early years of their sixty-two-year-long marriage, Frank, who recently passed away, repeatedly accommodated Eve's needs, relocating and leaving jobs so that they could be with her family in Melbourne, and later so that she could have a career.Despite 'trying to be a really, really good mum', Eve had become 'terribly bored and very, very unhappy' 95 raising her three children at home and then trying to balance her family's needs with own her need for self-fulfilment through involvement in the workforce.She had first attempted to run a family law practice from home, then tried part-time outside work with a solicitor.Later, both out of 'desperation' and the realisation that there must be other women like her, 96 she started up Mahlab Recruitment as 'an agency finding part-time work for women lawyers' 97 when her oldest child was seven and her youngest was under four.At the time, she regarded her situation as 'a personal struggle' rather than a feminist issue: 'I didn't see it as any sort of indirect discrimination … '. 98 Nor, at that stage, did she consider it 'radical' for Frank to give up his job, 99 'because it was incompatible with [her] having a career'. 100In retrospect, however, Eve came to the realisation that the practical role reversal that she and Frank implemented was ground-breaking for the 1960s, even though her life had been 'outwardly … traditional' and 'lived by the conventional, middle class bourgeois rules'. 101She added that our society 'puts an intolerable burden on mothers' 102 and ' … has to change'.'[F]amilies have to adjust so that women aren't so oppressed within them'. 103She cited her own family's adjustment to this non-traditional dynamic of considering her needs as important evidence against the view that ' … liberation has to be at the expense of the family'. 104evertheless, there are indications in Eve's narrative of a lingering uncertainty or insecurity about the choices she made and their impact on her family, particularly her children.While this sense was more palpable in her Tall Poppies interview, 105 recorded in 1982, when she was forty-five, closer to the situation and better able to recall her feelings, it resurfaced in her Trailblazing oral history, twenty-eight years later: I'd structured things so I was there structurally and physically but my mind was elsewhere.… And I think I wasn't there for them at a time when really I should have been, when they needed it 106 … they actually grew into decent people, despite the poor mothering they got from me. 107roughout the audio recording of her life narrative, Eve's diction is slow, measured, mostly unemphatic, even dispassionate at times.These vocal qualities portray her as reflective, 'up-front' and sincere.As in the preceding quotations, she repeatedly acknowledges the limits of her abilities as a mother, wife and daughter-in-law.Yet in a number of instances, these self-judgements are accompanied by laughter, perhaps betraying discomfort or embarrassment.The overtones of regret and/or perhaps guilt in Eve's comments echo the attitudes impressed on her as an adolescent and made most explicit by her mother, reminding us of Knauer's argument for the need to factor in the temporal aspect of identity formation, which means that an individual's self-perception and worldview 'do not always evolve at the same pace as broader social change … because outmoded forms of bias and subordination often linger and find expression' in the present. 108Eve's almost apologetic comments are also a reminder that motherhood and a career continue to involve competing interests for women and that this is a legacy of the deeply ingrained, often unconscious nature of social attitudes towards gender roles and thus of the ongoing patterns of socialisation of females and males.

In summary, Eve Mahlab's perceptions of the forces that shaped her life and consciousness have so far offered important insights into one of the questions posed in this research project, that is, how one trailblazing lawyer's generational context, social background-particularly familial influences, citizenship status, ethnicity, religionand prevailing cultural values intersected with her gender to impact on the type of legal practice most accessible to her and, later, on her acts of citizenship.In the following section, we examine Eve's reflections on the influence of law on her life, professional career and civic contributions.
Interactions with law

As foreshadowed in 2.2 above, our research also focuses on whether women lawyers chose their profession as a means to achieving gender equality, given the reform potential of law.As previously mentioned, Eve did not herself choose to do law and entered her degree as a 'pretty unfocused' sixteen-year-old and without a developed social consciousness-'I don't think I was particularly for anything'. 109Nor did she enter the profession with a view to bringing about social or even legal reform.As with some aspects of her private life-like her decision to have three children in rapid succession without 'independent critical thought' 110 -Eve's early interactions with law were accidental, a term that recurs in other trailblazing lawyers' framing of their life (e.g.Valerie French 111 ).Yet, over time, Eve did use her training and status as a lawyer in the service of legal, social and political reform, and further, came to acknowledge with gratitude the appropriateness of the choice.

In her oral history, Eve Mahlab reflected on the four ways that law influenced her life and career.First, through the knowledge foundation she acquired: ' … the law has given me … a framework' to 'make sense of the way society operates'. 112Of the subjects she most enjoyed studying, she singled out legal history and British history as enabling her to understand:
… how Australian democracy has come about … [U]ntil the fifties, all the migration was British and Irish.And they brought the assumptions about democracy with them.

… the history of democracy has been an expansion of human rights to wider and wider communities, you know, from the King to the nobles, from the nobles to the gentry, from the gentry to the people in trade, right?From the people in, in trade and business to the workers, and finally to women.

And … the push is now to have them extended to children at older ages, to lower … the age for voting.So it's been an expansion of rights that has been gradual.And, again, I don't think people understand that and how important it is … So that came … through my law course. 113 addition to this conceptual legacy, Eve's law studies endowed her with 'a certain consciousness' 114 that she was able to apply across her varied endeavours, from business to governance and philanthropy.She cited as examples raising the awareness of fellow Westpac board members to their need to have professional indemnity insurance in view of their personal liability for health and safety issues; 115 bringing to her feminist activism the ability to examine, criticise and propose legislative reform-the Family Law Act in 1975 116 and the Equal Opportunity for Women in the Workplace Act in 1999-because of concerns about the legal and financial implications for women; 117 and more recently, her scrutiny and amendments to a contract the Women Donors Network was negotiating with a sponsor. 118hird, legal training gave Eve a set of portable practical tools that she could equally use in business and in providing legal advice, among them, skills in 'basic analysis', 119 the ability to 'think logically' and to ' … argue by precedent … so you look at one set of circumstances and you … distil something from those.And you can apply them in another set of circumstances'; 120 and advocacy skills, which she also carried into public life:

We didn't have any formal training in advocacy at all.… But, nevertheless … you know, a client brings you … a set of circumstances and you look at … what affects them legally.And you … you blend that with the factual circumstances … And you give them some advice.And … it is a sort of advocacy.… And I think that … those skills … they're communication skills, in a way, and logical. 121nally, Eve Mahlab, like other trailblazers interviewed in this project, was conscious of the social and personal redressive power attached to her law degree.For Rosemary Kayess, for instance, the status and authority associated with law enabled her to overcome her powerlessness as a disabled woman. 122For Eve, law redressed a different source of powerlessness: Kim Rubenstein: … In the Susan Mitchell book, Tall Poppies, you talk about law as an option that would, and I'm quoting here, '[r]egain what had been lost in status and position' when your parents had become second-class citizens in Australia.

Eve Mahlab: That's true … there are so many law courses now … But … when I did law, which was in … 1954 … [i]t was really hard to get into law school.… I think Melbourne had the only law school in Victoria.

And so I joined an elite by having got into the law course.It meant that I … had a certain level of intelligence.And the networks that I developed were mainly men who became … well-known lawyers or judges, went into government.… And I think that, that sort of reflected on me and gave me a certain standing as well and enabled me to further my career and enhance my confidence.And, yeah, it was important to be a lawyer. 123 addition to her acknowledgement of the professional and personal skills that came from her legal training, Eve's reflections emphasise her awareness of the social status associated with lawyering, particularly at the time when she entered the profession, and of the credibility and access to the public sphere her participation in an elite, predominantly male, network gave her in the perceptions of others.Law offered her a bridge from the outsider, 'second class' status of refugee, female and 'rebel' to the inner circle of those with the power to effect legal and social reform.It was this sense of empowerment, along with her natural assertiveness and awakened feminist consciousness, that led to her becoming active in WEL, and that, nurtured by her involvement in this movement, gave her the profile to very deliberately redirect her career and participate in a range of public roles, some at her own behest.For example, Eve's appointment in 1975, and at the age of thirty-eight, to the Victorian Government Committee of Inquiry into the Status of Women-whose report 'led to anti-discrimination legislation' 124 -was, she recalled, no accident.Instead, she wrote to the then Victorian Premier who had established the Committee, suggesting that he appoint her as a member.Eve reflected on this achievement, saying, 'I'm sure I wouldn't have been appointed if I hadn't exactly asked, which is also a lesson, I think, for women, that you have to, you know, put yourself forward, 'cause it's so easy to overlook you.' 125 In short, law was her passport to active citizenship, since, by her own account, it provided her with the authority, training and confidence that enabled her to put herself forward for participation in the public sphere: Kim Rubenstein: And would it be fair to say, having the lawyering and that foundation … has enabled you to be an active [citizen?]Eve Mahlab: Absolutely, absolutely.I don't think I could … first, have the confidence but, secondly, have the skills to have done what I've done if I hadn't studied law, not so much practiced it, although that also added to it, particularly in the family law area, but studied it. 126alysis of Eve's oral history interview highlights her achievements in relation to gender equality, despite her acknowledgement that she did not initially enter a life of law for its reform potential.Nevertheless, her testimony informs the second last research focus outlined in 2.2, in indicating how the ability of lawyers to perform civic duty, 'to make a difference', is enhanced by the professional credibility associated with lawyering in the public realm and the resulting sense of authority with which it imbues lawyers, along with the tools gained with a legal education.
Eve's acts of citizenship: social and legal reform towards women's equality and empowerment

Several instances stand out among Eve's recollections of her social policy and law reform work from the time she joined WEL.In each case, she drew on her feminist consciousness, her legal status and/or training and her personal strength of character to bring about change.At times, she also brought her political aspirations and entrepreneurial creativity to bear on her work.The first of these, in 1974, involved lobbying the Manager of Victorian Railways over the exclusion of women from employment as train drivers.

Well, … the argument, I think, put forward by that man was that women could never drive a train … because, to be an engine driver, you had to have been a train guard.That was the career progression.And to be a train guard you had to be able to li-, lift 44-gallon drums.And women couldn't lift 44-gallon drums.And it's very interesting because … that thinking still pervades … First of all, I argued that 'What has lifting a 44-gallon drum got to do with an ability to drive a train?'And basically, it's just … a discriminatory exclusion, right? 127ound the same time, Eve was also instrumental in contributing to a submission from WEL to the Federal Senate Standing Committee on Constitutional and Legal Affairs, which was made up exclusively of male members.Eve and another female lawyer, Lyn Opas, examined the Family Law Bill 1973 and made submissions, as a result of which they were invited to meet with the then Federal Attorney General. 128Reforms to the Act ultimately included no-fault divorce: I'm not sure how much credit we can take but basically the Act … the Bill, as it stood, gave no credit for women's unpaid contribution in the house, you know, as a source of building family wealth.… it would've really disadvantaged women very much after divorce. 129e third example of Eve's involvement in social policy activism carried a deeply entrenched politicisation.In 1973, during a state election campaign, she was responsible for designing and chairing a WEL forum, called 'Why should women vote for you?'.Eve remembered that:

… it was such a … co-operative event.We all worked our butts off … through various connections that different WEL members had … And … some connections with the Liberal Party.… we got the leaders of the four parties who were fielding candidates in the state election … to answer questions that women had posed.They were questions about childcare and equal pay and contraception.… and there were 2000 women.It was, again, it was an incredibly exciting event.And WEL had no money.And I had met Ron Casey from Channel 7.And we went to him and they decided they'd film the whole thing.And it was on Channel 7.And there was such a demand, it was replayed within two or three days. 130rawing on her media connection with Ron Casey was one example of Eve's ability to draw on her entrepreneurial experience and networking skills to publicise and promote the WEL cause.Other instances of her ability to engage her business knowhow in the public sphere include initiating the ungendered KnowBis project, designed to broaden students' career opportunities.

Eve acknowledged that her family history had led her to view business 'as a very, very productive thing to do, and a very creative thing'. 131This continues, with her co-founding and ongoing involvement in the Women Donors Network mentioned earlier as a further example of her ability to bring her entrepreneurial knowledge into relationship with her commitment to women's equality.

A fifth set of examples reflects Eve Mahlab's advocacy for reform in the corporate domain to achieve equal treatment for women and family friendly practices in the workplace.As a member of the Monash University Council, she remembered having lobbied for childcare, succeeded in changing a meeting time to suit Council members with young children, and drawn attention to the 'subtle' bias against women candidates by selection committees. 132Similarly, as previously mentioned, she effectively used the prominence associated with her Businesswoman of the Year award in 1982 to advocate for workbased childcare provisions in the corporate sector.She related how in accepting the award, she gave a speech about how:

… childcare empowered women to move into the workforce.And equality was incredibly important … And one of the joys was that, sometime afterwards … Joan Ford, who … was working [for] Lend Lease or Esso at the time.… came to me and she said that, as a result of that speech, they had established a childcare centre.And it was … one of the first work-based childcare centres in, in Australia.And she said it had, again, been on the agenda for a long time.But she had been in the audience.And when she heard me she went back to her boss and said, 'You know, this has dropped off the agenda.We have to do it.'And they did. 133ain, as the inaugural female member of the Westpac Board in 1993, her first Board lunch was due to be held at a men's only venue.Eve told the chairman that she 'felt uncomfortable going to clubs which wouldn't have [her] as a member.And he was very understanding.And, as a result of that, he … said that Westpac would have no more … board lunches, at men's only … club [s] [sic]'. 134hese examples inform two Trailblazing Project research questions, providing insights into how Eve Mahlab was able to use her entrepreneurial background and her legal training-and/or the credibility associated with that training-to political effect to achieve social and legal reform towards assuring women's equal rights as citizens and employees.
Eve's self-perception of her acts of citizenship
Advocacy as active citizenship

In her Trailblazing oral history, Eve Mahlab identified her chief public contribution as one of advocacy, a skill she considered she had developed through giving clients legal advice, as mentioned earlier, and, like another trailblazing lawyer, Rosemary Kayess, 135 through 'giving voice' to disempowered members of society: I think in my case being an active citizen has been about advocacy, giving voice to a group of people, namely women, who don't have a voice, or not enough voice.… It's about giving ideas, putting ideas into the culture and, in some ways, developing them and spreading them, which will benefit wider groups of people. 136 her Tall Poppies interview, Eve explicitly acknowledged this motivation for her acts of citizenship and vowed to 'continue to fight so that other women ha[d] the same choices' 137 that had enabled her to overturn the status quo in her private life and to achieve a sense of self-fulfilment through her career.

Almost thirty years later, in her Trailblazing interview, as discussed in 4.1.3above, she elaborated on the parallel she perceives between the powerlessness experienced by her family due to their ethnicity and religion and by women, who 'historically have had little power'; and expressed her wish to 'add to … them getting more'. 138n the other hand, with characteristic honesty, Eve also admitted her second motivation towards advocacy: … I think most contribution is selfish.… I do, in theory, want to build a, a better and a fairer world.But I do this because I have a need to do it.I want to help other people but only in the way that I feel is enjoyable.And … I don't think I'm being quite fair to myself because there are always … things that you do that are not enjoyable but they have to be done in pursuit of your goal.So I do those as well.But I do have a gift related to clear thinking and advocacy that I use. 139sewhere she commented:

… you know, people do, if they're lucky, they do what they're good at.And I'm good at advocacy.I'm not good at detail.I'm not good … in the executive role.… I have a problem, you know, with filing things.And, and I'm … not terribly organised. 140 might be said that Eve's strengths-advocacy, public speaking, seeing the 'bigger picture', being entrepreneurial and a 'catalyst' for bringing together 'people who have common interests or, or might have a synergistic effect' 141 -are, especially in the context of her generation, more typically associated with men, whereas the attributes she identifies as her weaknesses are usually associated with women.This sense of her 'otherness' would seem to underlie her self-characterisation as someone who is 'very good at self-interest', 142 a statement that bears the same overtones of self-judgement as her remarks about her 'poor mothering' noted earlier.Here again, Eve's stance reminds us of the disjunct between her conscious attempts to overturn the status quo and her unconscious attitudes, as noted earlier (4.1.6),that may well be explained by Knauer's theory about the influence on identity formation of the socio-historical context, particularly in an individual's formative years. 143It equally raises questions about whether an ambitious man would feel the need to be apologetic about engaging in a career that dovetails with his strengths and/or that he finds most satisfying; and by extension, about the gendered norms surrounding success and contributions in public life, a question that will be taken up in the following section of this paper.

Eve's self-confessed motivations also highlight the extent to which her acts of citizenship represent an overturning of traditional gender roles in the public sphere, as did her family arrangements in the private sphere; and this, both fifty years ago and even, still, today, can be considered as a mould-breaking social contribution.In establishing Mahlab Recruitment, she had stepped off the conventional legal practice trail, in the first instance, to resolve her own need to find stimulating employment that was compatible with her family responsibilities.However, in drawing on her personal experience, she was also able to make the workplace more accessible to other female lawyers seeking part-time work compatible with their family commitments, 144 an endeavour which at times required her advocacy skills to break down sexist barriers in the legal profession:

… we saw ourselves as speaking for these women and being responsible for integrating them into the profession.… I remember one firm who … said they would never take a woman article clerk.And I remember saying to them, 'Look, there is this … woman.I would really, really like you to interview her.Now, of course, there's no obligation.'And they did.And they not only … gave her articles, but they came back to me afterwards and they said, 'From now on, we're only going to take women,' which is as stupid as the other.But that, you know, was the attitude'. 145terestingly, beyond these business activities, Eve's more targeted contributions to the fight for equality for women give us further insight into the way her legal trainingalloyed to her strengths as a pragmatist, advocate and courageous 'natural rebel', 146 as well as her networking skills, entrepreneurship and feminist consciousness-enabled her to feel confident about 'making waves' and influencing the public sphere.Eve's entrée into WEL, facilitated by her legal standing and her fellow committee members' perception of her authority, was pivotal to her advocacy career.Advocacy galvanised her, fulfilling a need for self-expression and perhaps, as well, for social recognition as an insider, that neither lawyering, nor marriage and motherhood-nor, at that point in time, her business ventures-was able to.But, in Eve's perception, law was the agent that catalysed this process: ' … my law knowledge and my being part of the … of the legal profession, has empowered me to make a difference, to try to make a difference … '. 147 Eve's outspokenness on feminist issues points to another feature of her trailblazing contribution which is her strength of character and consequent ability to swim against the tide.She became the spokesperson for WEL when other women were unable or unwilling to do so, because they feared their jobs were at risk or 'had internalised … middle class attitudes like not showing off or looking for publicity, and that there was something unfeminine about speaking out'. 148Eve was prepared to carry out this work, despite the risks it brought to her reputation-she felt she was 'branded a radical communist by the women who want to be women, for supporting anti-discrimination law reform' 149 -and to her business and her family, who even received a 'very serious bomb threat' as a result of her public profile. 150t a personal level, Eve had the courage to shoulder the guilt of being there for her children 'structurally and physically' while '[her] mind was elsewhere'; 151 and the strength of self to be able to live with uncertainty about the consequences of considering '[her] needs as important' 152 -which involved asking her family to accept her non-traditional roles as a wife and mother-and with the weight of public opinion about this divergence from convention.Eve's discussion of this aspect of her life in the private sphere is unvarnished.She reflected that her husband, Frank had 'put up with a lot', 153 and that:

… he had no problem with me going back to work as long as he and the children didn't suffer.And I thought that was very, very reasonable for many years, until I decided [laughter] that maybe they would suffer.And they just had to bear it (emphasis added). 154ile tenacity emerges as a common characteristic in trailblazing women lawyers' narratives, we again note Eve's striking use of the language of obligation, like the verbal construction 'had to' (above), to convey a lack of choice or agency (see 4.1.4above).It is, however, interesting to observe that, as Eve described having become more conscious, confident and influential on the public stage, her expressions of obligation signal her own power rather than her powerlessness: e.g. in her decision regarding her family (above), or when she was hired to investigate the need for cultural change to address discriminatory practices in a large stockbroking firm, and insisted that 'in order to have the necessary status and … for the project to be taken seriously, [she] had to have … an office next to the executive chairman' (emphasis added). 155Viewed in the light of distinctive features of Eve's narrative style, we can appreciate the force of the dynamic between powerless and power in her psyche, but also the extent to which her acts of citizenship required a 'cut and dried' pragmatism, that enabled her to make hard decisions and wear the consequences.
Service vs. contribution

The discussion of her various contributions led Eve to elaborate on her conception of different forms of active citizenship that she identified as belonging to the private or public spheres.Underpinning this discussion are echoes of Eve's self-judgements about her unconventional, 'unfeminine' strengths and interests and the notion of the culturally ingrained nature of attitudes towards gender roles in both spheres.These motifs resurface in the distinction she made between the concepts of 'service' and 'contribution'.
Eve Mahlab: I don't think I've been driven by giving service.I've been driven by what interests me (emphasis added).

Kim Rubenstein: … that statement that you just made that you … don't think you've been driven by service.Can we try and perhaps just develop that a little bit more?I mean, a, a strong theme is that you've been doing things that you've been interested in.But they've been in the public domain … or … for whatever reasons, they've become public.

Eve Mahlab: Yes … I guess … I see myself as an advocate.And an advocate for building a better world through women and girls.And that may have good effects over time.But I see service as much more close.I've never worked in a soup kitchen.I've never worked in a women's refuge.I've never actually been close up to alleviate pain or suffering.I hope that, in the long term, the things that I advocate for will do that.But face to face, I haven't done it. 156is discussion is noteworthy, because the areas Eve identified as service are those that are more directly linked to the private sphere of assisting people directly in their domestic needs-providing food in a soup kitchen, working with women fleeing domestic violence in a refuge.Her examples are areas of service and contribution that she qualified as involving 'care for society's victims-the aged, the children, the disabled' 157 -and that have more traditionally been undertaken by women.In her Tall Poppies interview, Eve had contrasted such contributions with the influence that she was able to wield through advocacy in positions in the public sphere:

When it comes to being part of governments, the number of women who have influence is absolutely infinitesimal.I suppose I'm amongst the few that do have it, but I don't have a lot.I can get a good hearing when I speak to people.I'm on various committees that make decisions so that I help just by being there and saying things like 'How does this affect women?Does it affect them differently from men? Are you assuming that all families are traditional with the woman at home and, if so, shouldn't we question that?'If you can ask those questions at the time when decisions are made, rather than jumping up and down after they have been made, I think you can be influential. 158e distinction Eve made over twenty-five years ago between men's 'positions of paid power' and women's 'positions of unpaid influence' 159 has in her mind, become more fixed over time.In a personal communication almost three years after the Trailblazing interview, she was keen to further make the distinction that the word 'service' in her mind was linked to 'servitude', adding that her sense of her own contribution was not about being a servant to others, but rather leading others. 160Her strong reaction to that concept is perhaps linked to the imbalance of power that 'servitude' represents and a reaction to that imbalance.Her resistance to the word 'service' and her desire for her contributions to be characterised as leadership may be an example of Eve having been consciously influenced by, and having adopted, what we might identify as gendered distinctions, where being active in the public sphere is more powerful and reflects the ability to exercise power.It is less personal-less individualistic-less about service.

And yet, the self-judgemental echo and the qualification of public contributions as 'selfish' 161 again point to the continuing unconscious influence on Eve of traditional attitudes to gendered roles and suggest that such attitudes remain a challenge that must be overcome by women who engage in the public sphere through acts of citizenship more generally.

The discussion also raises some thought-provoking questions about the way we think about gender and citizenship: Does Eve's conception of service play into the way the public sphere has also been gendered-that it is less personal, gendered through representing male norms around power and leadership and less service orientated?Does this equate with the public sphere being about men and power, and the private sphere being about women's submission and servitude?If women's major public contributions have been traditionally conceived of as service rather than leadership, then it reflects a more gendered concept of citizenship that women have not been part of.Here again, the Trailblazing Project allows us to enlarge our thinking of active citizenship to include 'service' and to contextualise the meaning of words outside of their gendered context, in the way that Eve resists. 162ore generally, the distinction made by Eve between service and contributions of influence and her identification with having played a leadership role through her acts of citizenship increase our awareness of what trailblazers' different ways of retelling their experiences reveal about their position within the legal and Australian culture. 163n this respect, it is interesting to note that Eve's self-perception of her public role and indeed her outspokenness diverge from the way other trailblazing women lawyers have conceived of and expressed their political and civic contributions in the public domain.For example, a repeated theme in the life narrative of Valerie French was her determined dismissal of conscious leadership, despite her involvement in a number of key reforms. 164The same can be said of Rosemary Kayess, who always described herself as nominated by others to positions of leadership. 165Both women can perhaps be seen as adopting a more traditional, 'feminine' stance of backgrounding one's own importance and rather emphasising the importance of others in their career trajectory and achievements, conforming to Conway's finding of the non-strategic aspect of trailblazing women's successes and to her assertion of deep, gendered continuities in the memoirs of these women. 166ve Mahlab's narrative diverges from this pattern.In contrast to French, beyond her early, accidental steps, by her late thirties, Eve's consciousness changed once she had 'found [her] home' in WEL: 167 the direction of her career became more deliberate as she began building on her public profile and drawing on women's networks to actively seek out an assume leadership roles.Furthermore, in recounting a rich number of experiences of advocacy and leadership, in both her Tall Poppies interview and Trailblazing oral history, she was willing to publicly own her ability to influence decisions that impacted on the rights of women and families.This evidence sheds light on the last research question noted in 2.2 (above), 168 adding to the focus on diversity and consistency in the Trailblazing Project, particularly regarding the issue of narrative style, an area that will continue to be of interest in analysing the oral histories of other women at the legal frontier, both in Australia and internationally.
Conclusions and significance of Eve Mahlab's oral history

Following the aims of this paper set out in 1.1, our study of Eve Mahlab's interview and life narrative-involving repeated close reading and itemised recording of relevant references-has shown how the Trailblazing Project provides data that substantially increases our understanding of the diverse experience of Australian women lawyers' professional lives and gives voice to their previously silenced stories.In particular, the examination of Eve's life narrative has shed light on the challenge involved in women's participation in the civic space, but, equally, on the formative influences that led to the development, over time, of one trailblazing woman lawyer's identity, political consciousness and profile, enabling her to largely overcome that challenge to make an impact on that space and on the history of Australian women's rights.

Several motifs emerge from our analysis.The first relates to Eve's perception that significant among the influences enhancing her civic contributions were the examples of courage, perseverance and entrepreneurship set by her parents and grandparents, as well as her acute sensitivity to the powerlessness attached to being a refugee and from a different ethnic and religious background.A second related motif involves Eve's keenly felt sense of being the 'Other' amongst her peers, because of her family background and later, her gender, activism, business endeavours and political orientation: 'It's been my fate to always be an outsider, not quite to belong'. 169These influences shaped her determination to achieve, her passion for entrepreneurship and her fight against disempowerment resulting from loss of citizenship and/or gender inequality.In stark contrast, the third motif concerns Eve's awareness of the professional authority and public influence accorded to lawyers and, although it was not one of Eve's motivations for becoming a lawyer, the reform potential of law.Empowered by this understanding, and by her access to the support of an elite, mainly male legal network and, especially, of female, and particularly feminist, networks, she used her legal training to political effect, particularly her skills in advocacy and in arguing from precedent.She was able to harness her legal knowledge to her natural assertiveness and the confidence associated with her status as a lawyer, in advocating socio-legal reform for an equality of citizenship for women and, through Mahlab Recruitment, in influencing the lives of other women lawyers as public actors.The final motif concerns the disjunct between Eve's pioneering behaviour in the private and public spheres and her more unconsciously held conventional attitudes to gendered roles. 170n regard to the second aim of this study, the analysis of Eve Mahlab's Trailblazing life narrative showcases the value of oral history as a research tool and method in legal scholarship: it not only identifies Eve's contributions to the history of women's rights in Australia to add them to the public record and public consciousness, 171 but her reflections also represent a first-hand account that enables us to understand, interpret and assess the social and professional forces that have shaped her and the motivations for her actions in the public and private spheres.In addition, the substance and style of her life narrative provides us with otherwise inaccessible insights into Eve's own understanding of her position in the national culture and in the history of its gender equality movement and of legal participation in this movement. 172urthermore, in terms of the reliability of oral history as a methodology, the availability of Eve's Tall Poppies interview as well as her Trailblazing recording, separated by some twenty-eight years, has allowed us to trace the evolution of her consciousness over time-with some of her positions becoming more fluid and others more fixedand, to some extent, to compensate for an inherent weakness in life narrative, which is the changed tangibility and texture of the subject's memories and perceptions when articulated from a distance. 173inally, again from a methodological perspective, the comparisons made with information drawn from the oral histories of other women pioneers interviewed for the Trailblazing Project, and/or documented in existing studies, amplify Eve's recollections of her lived experiences, placing them in the chronological context of those of other Australian women lawyers of her generation and beyond, and also providing some preliminary reflections on the gendered nature of storytelling. 174ith the full quota of Trailblazing life narrative recordings now completed, and the analysis of these now underway, the project has already hinted at oral history's ability to foster the equal representation of women in public memory and to reflect on how women tell their own stories.Our continuing study of these life recordings can weave women's remarkable actions into the national identity and provide women with an enlarged national space to inhabit, reflect and imagine their diverse experiences.
